title: Enough is a number you pick.
dek: Two people get the same raises for six years. The one who decided what enough was saved 2.5 times more.
whyThisIdea: Am sărit peste ideile 7–16 pentru că ultimele șase propuneri au fost toate despre obiceiuri și studiu, iar „Nobody tells you when to start” se suprapune mult cu articolul despre Monday. Asta revine la bani și se leagă direct de citatul tău preferat din recenzia „The Psychology of Money” („Knowing when you have enough”), cu un calcul simplu: aceleași măriri de salariu, de 2,5 ori mai mulți bani economisiți.

entry.title: Enough is a number you pick.
entry.titleHtml: Enough is a number you pick.
entry.dek: Two people get the same raises for six years. The one who decided what enough was saved 2.5 times more.
body: “The hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving.” — Morgan Housel

Have you ever asked yourself how much money would be enough for you? Not “more”, not “a lot”, an actual number. I tried, and the first thing I noticed is that I had never done it before. In the review of “The Psychology of Money” here, the quote I picked as my favourite ends with three words: knowing when you have enough. I liked it so much that I put it at the bottom of the article, and then I never asked myself what my enough is. So the question is: can you pick “enough” before you have much of anything? Let’s start from the beginning.

The story Housel uses for this is one of my favourites in the whole book. The writers Kurt Vonnegut and Joseph Heller (the author of “Catch-22”) were at a party at the house of a billionaire on Shelter Island, near New York. Vonnegut asked Heller how it felt to know that their host may have made more money in one day than “Catch-22” had made in its whole history. Heller said he had something the host could never have. And when Vonnegut asked what that was, Heller answered: “The knowledge that I’ve got enough.” Vonnegut wrote it down as a short poem, published in The New Yorker in 2005, six years after Heller died.

Firstly, let’s look at the word itself, because I think it is a strange one. “Enough” sounds like a full stop - you arrive, and the sentence ends. But for most people it is not a full stop, it is a direction. When you have 100, enough is 200. When you have 200, enough is 400. Housel says the hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving, and the important word there is not “goalpost”, it is moving. Enough is not a place you reach, it is a number you have to decide on, or it keeps running away from you. Nobody hands it to you. If you do not pick it yourself, the people around you and the things you see every day will pick it for you.

Secondly, let’s put some numbers on the moving goalpost, and I want to be clear that this is an example I built, not a prediction. Two people earn $1.000 a month and spend $900, so they both save $100, which is 10%. Every year, both of them get a 10% raise (a lot, I know, I picked it so the numbers stay easy). The first person lets the spending grow exactly as fast as the income, so he always saves 10%. The second person decides that $900 is close to enough, and only lets the spending grow by 3% a year.
Monthly income in year 6: $1.000 × 1.15 = about $1.611 for both
First person in year 6: spends $1.449, saves $161
Second person in year 6: spends $1.043, saves $567
Saved in total over the six years: $9.259 against $22.728

Read the last line twice. Same job, same raises, and the second person saved about 2.5 times more. And he did not live like a monk either - his spending still went up by almost 16% in those six years. The difference is that the first person’s spending went up by 61%, exactly as much as the income, so after six years of raises he has nothing extra to show for them except a more expensive month. The raise was the same for both of them. Only one of them actually got to keep it. I left out taxes and prices going up, so read it as the shape of the thing, not as a forecast.

Thirdly, the part of the chapter that is not about saving at all, and I think it is the real reason Housel cares about this word. He opens the chapter with Rajat Gupta, a man who grew up in India, became the head of McKinsey, one of the most famous consulting firms in the world, and sat on the board of Goldman Sachs. He was already rich by any normal measure. In 2012 he was convicted of insider trading and sentenced to two years in prison, for passing secret information from that board to a hedge fund manager. Housel’s line about it is one of the best in the book: “There is no reason to risk what you have and need for what you don’t have and don’t need.” Not knowing what enough is does not only cost you savings, sometimes it costs you everything you already had.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. I am a student, so I do not have a salary to protect yet. But I do have a month, and a month has a number. I will write down what my month actually costs right now, and next to it one sentence: this is enough for this part of my life. Then, the next time I have more money than usual, a summer job or a birthday, I will look at that paper before I decide what the extra money is for. Not to forbid anything, just so the goalpost moves only when I move it.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the idea is right, but I have to be honest about who is saying it. It is very easy to talk about enough when you are young and do not have much to lose. People who struggle to pay their rent do not need a lecture about enough, they need more. And the research does not say money stops mattering either. In 2010, Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton found that how good people feel day to day stops rising at about $75.000 a year. Then in 2021, Matthew Killingsworth found that it keeps rising. In 2023 Killingsworth and Kahneman worked together, with Barbara Mellers, and found that the plateau is real only for the least happy people, at around $100.000, and for most people more money keeps helping. So enough is not “money does not matter”. What I take from it is smaller: <u>more can keep helping you, as long as you are the one who decides where the line is</u>.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“The hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving.” — Morgan Housel
